The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set,
$0<r<1$, and let $q$ be a measurable real function on $U$. Define
$$[q]_{H^r(U)}^2:=\int_U\int_U\frac{|q(x)-q(y)|^2}{|x-y|^{d+2r}}\,dx\,dy,$$
with the diagonal integrand set to zero, and
$H^r(U):=\{q\in L^2(U):[q]_{H^r(U)}<\infty\}$, using almost-everywhere
classes and norm $\|q\|_{H^r(U)}^2:=\|q\|_{L^2(U)}^2+[q]_{H^r(U)}^2$.
For $u\in H^1(U)$, write $u\in H^{1+r}(U)$ when each weak derivative
$\partial_j u$ belongs to $H^r(U)$, and define
$$|u|_{H^{1+r}(U)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^d[\partial_j u]_{H^r(U)}^2.$$
For vector fields, use the sum of the componentwise squared $H^r$ norms.
Use these definitions on each cell $K$ and on the full domain $\Omega$, with
$\|u\|_{H^{1+r}(U)}^2:=\|u\|_{H^1(U)}^2+|u|_{H^{1+r}(U)}^2$. At $r=1$,
set $H^1(U)=W^{1,2}(U)$, interpret $[q]_{H^1(U)}^2:=\|\nabla q\|_{L^2(U)}^2$,
and set $H^{1+r}(U)=W^{2,2}(U)$ with the ordinary integer-order norm and
membership of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. Thus
$|u|_{H^2(U)}^2=\sum_{j,k}\|\partial_k\partial_j u\|_{L^2(U)}^2$. The local
seminorm is the restriction of the Slobodeckij convention in
[[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]] to $U\times U$.

$$\|\gamma_Fq\|_{L^2(F)} \le C\left(h_K^{-1/2}\|q\|_{L^2(K)} +h_K^{r-1/2}[q]_{H^r(K)}\right),$$

If $u\in H^1(K)$, $\nabla u\in H^r(K;\mathbb R^d)$, and

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: On $0<x<1/4$, writing $c(y)=y(1-y)$, one has $\partial_xu=\tfrac34c(y)x^{-1/4},\qquad \partial_yu=(1-2y)x^{3/4}.$ Everywhere else the cutoff and its derivative are bounded. Since $u$ and $\partial_yu$ are square integrable and $|\partial_xu|^2\le C(1+x^{-1/2})$, the weak first derivatives lie in $L^2(\Omega)$; the classical interior derivatives give the distributional derivatives because test functions are compactly supported away from the boundary. Thus $u\in H^1(\Omega)$.

To prove the zero-boundary condition, let $\theta_\epsilon(t):=\sigma((t-\epsilon)/\epsilon)$. By [F1], it is smooth, zero for $t\le\epsilon$, and one for $t\ge2\epsilon$. Since $\sigma'$ is continuous and vanishes outside $[0,1]$, $\|\theta_\epsilon'\|_\infty\le C/\epsilon$. Set $\eta_\epsilon(x,y)=\theta_\epsilon(x)\theta_\epsilon(y)\theta_\epsilon(1-y)$. Each $\eta_\epsilon u$ is smooth and compactly supported in $\Omega$, since the $x$ cutoff removes the only nonsmooth boundary point and $\chi$ vanishes near $x=1$. Write $u-\eta_\epsilon u=(1-\theta_\epsilon(x))u+\theta_\epsilon(x)(1-\theta_\epsilon(y)\theta_\epsilon(1-y))u$. In the first term, all support lies in $x<2\epsilon$; the squared $L^2$ and derivative errors are bounded by $C\epsilon^{2(3/4)-1}=C\epsilon^{1/2}$, including the $\epsilon^{-1}u$ cutoff derivative. In the second term, support lies in the two strips of width $2\epsilon$ near $y=0,1$. There $|u|\le Cx^{3/4}\operatorname{dist}(y,\{0,1\})$ and its first derivatives are bounded by $Cx^{3/4}+Cx^{-1/4}\operatorname{dist}(y,\{0,1\})$; integrating the strips shows the squared errors and cutoff-derivative terms are $O(\epsilon)$. Thus $\eta_\epsilon u\to u$ in $H^1(\Omega)$, so the closure definition gives $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$.

Choose $0<\delta<1/12$ so small that $c(y')/c(y)\le1.05$ whenever $0<x<\delta$, $1/3\le y\le2/5$, and $y\le y'\le y+x$. For the pairs below, $x'\le3x<1/4$, so both points lie where $\chi=1$; also $c(y)$ is bounded below by a positive constant on this $y$ interval. For $2x\le x'\le3x$ and $y\le y'\le y+x$, the values of $\partial_xu(x,y)$ and $\partial_xu(x',y')$ then differ by at least $\tfrac34c(y)x^{-1/4}\bigl(1-1.05\,2^{-1/4}\bigr).$ Thus $|\partial_xu(x,y)-\partial_xu(x',y')|\ge Cx^{-1/4}$. Also $|(x,y)-(x',y')|\le\sqrt5x$. By [F2], restricting the $H^{1/2}$ Gagliardo integral to these pairs gives a lower bound $C\int_0^\delta x^{-1/2}x^{-3}\,x^2\,dx =C\int_0^\delta x^{-3/2}\,dx=\infty,$ where the two factors of $x$ are the lengths of the $x'$ and $y'$ intervals. Thus $\partial_xu\notin H^{1/2}(\Omega)$.

Let $D=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)=\sqrt2$. For $1/2<r<1$ and $x\ne y$, $|x-y|^{-3}=|x-y|^{2r-1}|x-y|^{-2-2r}\le D^{2r-1}|x-y|^{-2-2r}$. Integrating gives $[q]_{H^{1/2}(\Omega)}^2\le D^{2r-1}[q]_{H^r(\Omega)}^2$ for every $q\in H^r(\Omega)$, so $H^r(\Omega)\subset H^{1/2}(\Omega)$. If $u\in H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ for such an $r$, [F4] would imply $\partial_xu\in H^r(\Omega)$ and hence $H^{1/2}(\Omega)$, contradicting step 2.1. Thus no exponent $r\in(1/2,1)$ satisfies the refuted claim.

It remains to exclude $r=1$. For $0<x<1/4$, the cutoff is one and $-\Delta u=	frac{3}{16}c(y)x^{-5/4}+2x^{3/4}$. On $1/3\le y\le2/5$, $c(y)$ is bounded below by a positive number, so this classical Laplacian is bounded below by $c_0x^{-5/4}$ for some $c_0>0$; its square has divergent integral at $x=0$. Since the distributional Laplacian agrees with this classical function in the open square, it has no $L^2$ representative. By [F5], $u
otin H^2(\Omega)=W^{2,2}(\Omega)$. The example still defines a bounded weak functional on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ by $v\mapsto\int_\Omega
abla u\cdot
abla v$, using Holder [F5]; it does not supply the $L^2$ source assumed by the method. Since the example has no $H^{1+r}$ regularity with $r>1/2$, it does not satisfy the trace hypothesis in [F3], and no normal-gradient trace conclusion is claimed.
Step 3.1 excludes every $r\in(1/2,1)$, and step 3.2 excludes $r=1$. These are all exponents in the asserted range, so the counterexample refutes the Statement.
